connector: Harriet will never sit in a classroom. The law and the plantation make sure of that. But in this chapter, called School Days, she is learning all the time: in the fields, under the big oak tree, in the woods. Count her teachers as you read, and ask yourself what kind of school this really is.

a.raw: the old slaves sang quiet songs about the bright north star and the long journey
a.fixed: The old slaves sang quiet songs about the bright North Star and the long journey.
a.why: Capital T to start; capital N and S on North Star (a specific named star); the adjectives old, quiet, bright and long all describe nouns in this sentence.

b.raw: daddy ben showed harriet the green moss on the tall trees
b.fixed: Daddy Ben showed Harriet the green moss on the tall trees.
b.why: Capitals on the names Daddy Ben and Harriet; the adjectives green and tall describe the nouns moss and trees; a period at the end.

fill1.h1: A balloon getting bigger pushes outward on every side. Which part means out?
fill1.why: ex- means out: ex + pand = to stretch out, to get bigger.

fill2.h1: Saying how you feel pushes it out of you and into words. Which part means out?
fill2.why: ex- means out: ex + press = to push out.

fill3.h1: This is the time that comes once a war is over. Which part means after?
fill3.why: post- means after: post + war = after the war.

fill4.h1: This happens once the final whistle has blown. Which part means after?
fill4.why: post- means after: post + game = after the game.

g4w20cf1.h1: Which word from the bank tells how wide the path is?
g4w20cf1.why: narrow tells the reader something new: there is only a little room on that path.

g4w20cf2.h1: Ground that cracks under boots is hard and icy. Which word tells you the season?
g4w20cf2.why: frozen tells the reader it is winter and the ground is hard.

g4w20cf3.h1: Which word from the bank tells how hard the bundle is to carry?
g4w20cf3.why: heavy tells the reader the bundle is hard to carry.

g4w20cf4.h1: What would a house sound like if nobody were home?
g4w20cf4.why: silent: no sound at all is the clue that nobody is there.

s4w20cf1.h1: Say Maryland slowly. What is the very first beat?
s4w20cf1.why: Mar·y·land: the first chunk is Mar, before the y sound.

s4w20cf2.h1: Say Delaware slowly. What is the very first beat?
s4w20cf2.why: Del·a·ware: the first chunk is Del.

s4w20cf3.h1: Underground starts with a little word that means not. What is it?
s4w20cf3.why: Un·der·ground: the first chunk is Un.

s4w20cf4.h1: Railroad is two words joined together. What is the first one?
s4w20cf4.why: Rail·road: two words, one beat each.

notes.wgrd: A chapter title is a clue to the central idea, and so is anything the writer shows more than once. Tally what repeats, then finish the sentence: this chapter is mostly about…
vocab: A large farm where one crop is grown (in the South, often using slave labor).
A true book about someone’s life, written by another person.
To stretch out or reach further.
To put off until a later time.
notes.wordParts: ex- means “out of” or “former,” and post- means “after”: exit, extend, postpone, postscript.
notes.grammar: An adjective describes a noun. It is worth adding only if it tells the reader something new: a cold spring tells the season. Cut adjectives that could describe almost anything.
notes.spelling: To split a long name, find the vowels, split between the consonants, and read each chunk. Names follow the same rules as any other word: Bal·ti·more.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. Harriet never goes to school. So how does she learn anything at all? That’s the question for Chapter 3, which Sterling calls School Days. Today you’ll warm up, practice adding describing words that do real work, read the chapter, and narrow your research to one question. Keep track of every teacher you meet.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Freedom Watch is about learning what you’re not supposed to know. In Harriet’s world, the law kept enslaved people from learning to read. But learning found other ways in: through stories, through songs, through news whispered from cabin to cabin. Watch how much Harriet learns without a single book.
transcripts.read: There’s no schoolhouse in Chapter 3, but there are teachers everywhere. Notice the old man who can read, and what he reads aloud. Notice the songs, and what they might really mean. And notice the walks in the woods near the end. What is Harriet learning there that no book could teach her?

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: going out, or coming after?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, saves scraps of cloth from the Big House and sews them, late at night by the fire, into a patchwork quilt of green and brown and yellow. It is the family’s only treasure. ex- means out, and post- means after. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. ex- = out, post- = after.

songs.title: Go Down, Moses
songs.heard: A Bible story about Moses leading the people of Israel out of Egypt, sung under the oak tree on Sunday.
songs.meant: Egypt was the plantation and Pharaoh was the master. “Let my people go” was a prayer for their own freedom.
songs.q: Later in the chapter, Master says anyone who sings “Go Down, Moses” will be whipped. What does that tell you he understood?
songs.a: He knew the song was not only about long-ago Egypt. It was about the people singing it, and about being free.

songs.title: Steal Away
lines: I ain’t got long to stay here.
songs.heard: A quiet hymn. The overseer swings his legs, nods along, and decides there is no trouble here.
songs.meant: A signal. When Cudjoe sang it, everyone knew there would be a secret meeting in the woods that night.
songs.q: Why is a song a safe way to send a message when the overseer is listening?
songs.a: Singing was allowed, even wanted. Words he already knew sounded harmless, so he never guessed they carried a plan.

songs.title: Didn’t My Lord Deliver Daniel
songs.heard: A Bible song about Daniel being saved from the lions.
songs.meant: A question aimed at their own lives: if Daniel was set free, why not every person held in slavery?
songs.q: The workers sing the last line louder each time. Why might Sterling end that scene on “Why not every man?”
songs.a: It is the question the whole book asks, and the people singing it are asking it about themselves.

ft.songsIntro: In Chapter 3, Harriet learns that singing is something like smiling: the white folks wanted the enslaved people to sing. But some songs said one thing to the overseer and something else to the people singing them.
